extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, critics, and aspiring novelists / readers learning how to analyse or write novels
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance on how to read, evaluate, and construct novels by examining their constituent 'aspects' (Story, People, Plot, Fantasy, Prophecy, Pattern, Rhythm). Emphasizes what each aspect contributes and common virtues/faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven Aspects of the Novel
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic selects seven distinct aspects by which to consider novels: The Story; People; The Plot; Fantasy; Prophecy; Pattern; Rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these seven named aspects as a framework for analysis — treat each as a separate dimension of a novel's achievement. The lecture frames subsequent discussion around these aspects and treats them as the primary lenses for criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story (fundamental aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence; it is the fundamental, indispensable backbone common to all novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a story by its singular merit: whether it makes the audience want to know what happens next; and its sole fault: whether it causes the audience not to want to know. Treat the story as the primitive spine of the novel — necessary but lowliest among literary organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time‑sequence requirement (life in time vs life by values)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story narrates the life in time (events in chronological order). Novels should also, if possible, include the 'life by values' — experiences measured by intensity rather than chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist must retain some thread of time inside the work; manipulating or bending chronological order is legitimate (e.g., Sterne, Proust), but wholly abolishing time risks unintelligibility. Aim to balance time-sequence narration with devices that convey value/intensity so the novel is more than mere chronological succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense / curiosity (the weapon of the storyteller)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense — keeping the reader wondering 'what will happen next?' — is the central tool of story-telling and often the primary source of reader engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should note how skillfully a novelist manages suspense (Scheherazade as exemplar). Strong storytelling often depends on the primitive curiosity of the audience; absence of suspense weakens the story even if other elements are competent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storyteller techniques vs plotted structure (ragged ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: A storyteller's method permits digressions, 'ragged ends' and episodes that do not necessarily tighten into a strict causal plot; this differs from a tightly constructed plot‑weaver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that digressive material can be an acceptable and even profitable feature of storytelling — it can sustain curiosity and colour the narrative — but overuse can slacken emotion and depth. Evaluate whether such looseness aids the novel's life-in-time or merely produces shallowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and Read‑Aloud Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The story-as-voice is the aspect of the novelist's work that asks to be read aloud; its appeal is primarily to the ear rather than to the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the opening sentences and narrative voice gain from oral delivery and whether the 'voice' adds to reader engagement. Note that while voice is valuable, it is not as decisive as deeper agencies (characters, plot, commentary) in conveying the author's personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of Space / Place (as alternative to time)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong sense of space — accumulation of place, landscape, and geographical scale — can be a dominant formal principle (e.g., Tolstoy's War and Peace) and generate grandeur distinct from time-sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, consider whether the novel's magnitude arises from spatial breadth as much as (or more than) temporal procession. Space can create musical-sounding effects and elevate the work beyond mere chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: People / Characters — revealing inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in a novel are constructed 'word-masses' that can be given inner life and made fully intelligible to the reader; the novelist's chief function is to reveal the hidden inner life that history cannot record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters on how convincingly the novelist exposes inner motives, thoughts, and 'romanesque' side (dreams, joys, sorrows) rather than only external actions. Characters may be more definite than real people because the novelist can disclose inner states; evaluate whether this disclosure is artful and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning characters into memoirs / historical doppelgängers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character is exactly identical to a real person (e.g., Queen Victoria exactly reproduced), the work becomes memoir or history rather than a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters remain imaginative creations informed by evidence + the novelist's temperament (the 'unknown quantity'). Maintain a degree of invention — do not reproduce real persons verbatim — to preserve the novel's fictional status and creative freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core human facts as tools for character-making (birth, food, sleep, love, death)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five obvious facts of human life — birth, food, sleep, love and death — are central raw material for novels; a novelist may reproduce, exaggerate, minimize, or reconfigure these in characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or assessing characters, consider how the novelist uses these elemental facts: Are they rendered accurately, transformed for thematic value, or used melodramatically? The writer's choices about these fundamentals affect realism, intensity and the reader's identification.
